## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with hypertension on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and disease relevance. Most notably, the direct enrichment of regulation of blood pressure (Gene Ontology:0008217, p = 1.44 × 10−8, 21 associated proteins) strongly supports the view that the prioritized protein set captures core mechanisms involved in vascular tone, fluid balance, and circulatory homeostasis. This interpretation is further complemented by the phenotype terms hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0002615, p = 1.80 × 10−2, 17 proteins) and orthostatic hypotension (Human Phenotype Ontology:0001278, p = 4.53 × 10−2, 9 proteins), which together suggest that many of the same molecular regulators may contribute to blood pressure instability across both hypertensive and hypotensive states. In turn, this pattern is consistent with published work indicating shared involvement of endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and altered vasoactive signaling.

Building on this hemodynamic theme, the enrichment profile also points to a broader inflammatory context that may interact with blood pressure regulation.

A second major theme is inflammation and immune activation. The very strong enrichment of overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WikiPathways:5095, p = 4.22 × 10−18, 39 proteins), neutrophil degranulation (Reactome:R-HSA-6798695, p = 7.35 × 10−15, 67 proteins), and signaling by interleukins (Reactome:R-HSA-449147, p = 3.66 × 10−8, 53 proteins) indicates that inflammatory cytokine networks and innate immune cell activation are central features of the hypertension-associated signature. This interpretation agrees with a large body of literature showing that interleukin signaling, leukocyte recruitment, and neutrophil-derived proteases and oxidants can promote endothelial injury, vascular stiffness, renal sodium retention, and sustained elevation of arterial pressure. The enrichment of viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04061, p = 7.44 × 10−20, 35 proteins) further reinforces the apparent importance of cytokine-receptor systems, even though this pathway is annotated in an infectious context.

Taken together, these immune-related signals appear to connect naturally with structural changes in the vessel wall and surrounding tissue environment.

A third prominent component involves extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue fibrosis. External encapsulating structure (Gene Ontology:0030312, p = 4.46 × 10−39, 93 proteins), collagen metabolic process (Gene Ontology:0032963, p = 2.91 × 10−9, 18 proteins), glycosaminoglycan binding (Gene Ontology:0005539, p = 4.63 × 10−15, 34 proteins), and carbohydrate binding (Gene Ontology:0030246, p = 5.06 × 10−15, 29 proteins) together point to marked alterations in matrix composition, proteoglycan interactions, and cell-surface adhesion biology. These findings are highly relevant because vascular fibrosis, collagen accumulation, and remodeling of the arterial wall are well-established contributors to increased vascular resistance and reduced compliance in hypertension. The associated enrichment of lysosome (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes:04142, p = 1.41 × 10−9, 28 proteins) also fits with prior literature linking lysosomal processing to inflammatory turnover, matrix degradation, and vascular remodeling.

Beyond these broadly shared vascular and inflammatory processes, the dataset also contains tissue-enriched signals that may reflect more specialized biological contexts.

Finally, tissue-enriched signals from placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (Human Protein Atlas:0381223, p = 6.13 × 10−7, 26 proteins) and duodenum; endocrine cells[greater than or equal to Low] (Human Protein Atlas:0151291, p = 2.99 × 10−7, 50 proteins) may reflect specialized secretory and barrier-associated proteins that participate in endocrine, inflammatory, and vascular regulation. The placental signal is particularly notable in light of the established relationship between placental dysfunction, endothelial injury, and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, whereas the endocrine cell signal may point more tentatively to hormone-mediated regulation of vascular and metabolic homeostasis. Overall, the pathway pattern supports a model in which hypertension may arise from the convergence of blood pressure regulatory mechanisms, chronic inflammation, cytokine signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tissue-specific endocrine or vascular responses, with many of these enrichments showing very strong statistical support across 18 to 93 associated proteins.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (HPA:0381223) 

The pathway described as placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[high] refers to the highly specialized apical surface of syncytiotrophoblasts that lines the chorionic villi of the placenta and is densely covered by microvilli. This microvillous membrane forms the principal maternal-facing exchange interface of the placenta and is essential for nutrient uptake, ion transport, peptide handling, endocrine signaling, barrier integrity, and communication between the placenta and the maternal circulation. Because syncytiotrophoblasts are directly exposed to maternal blood, their microvilli are not only structural amplifiers of surface area but also active signaling platforms enriched in membrane proteins, cytoskeletal components, glycocalyx molecules, and extracellular vesicle release machinery. The cited literature indicates that this compartment is highly sensitive to placental ischemia, oxidative stress, and abnormal trophoblast differentiation in hypertensive pregnancy. Earlier ultrastructural studies showed that placentas from pregnancies complicated by hypertension display reduced microvillar density, decreased intramembranous particles, reduced actin content in the microvillar cytoskeleton, and other features interpreted as syncytiotrophoblast immaturity or injury, changes likely to impair maternal-fetal exchange and membrane signaling (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:2792915, PubMed:6754249). Additional work demonstrated increased lipid peroxidation in syncytiotrophoblast microvillous plasma membranes in pregnancy-induced hypertension, supporting the view that oxidative damage to this membrane domain contributes to placental dysfunction and maternal vascular injury (PubMed:8035780). More recent evidence extends this concept from morphology to mechanism by showing that syncytiotrophoblast-derived extracellular vesicles carry pathogenic cargo, including neprilysin, from the placental surface into the maternal circulation, where they can directly impair vasodilatory signaling and induce preeclamptic hypertension (PubMed:40304042). Reduced syndecan-1 expression on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli in preeclampsia further suggests disturbance of the placental glycocalyx at this surface, linking microvillous injury to altered maternal vascular adaptation (PubMed:27299886).

Taken together, these observations provide a useful framework for interpreting why this placental surface compartment may be relevant to hypertension-associated molecular enrichment.

The collected publications support a model in which the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous pathway is closely linked to hypertension in pregnancy because this placental surface is both a target of placental stress and a source of factors that drive maternal vascular dysfunction. Classical morphologic studies consistently reported that hypertensive placentas show fewer syncytiotrophoblast microvilli, lower actin content, reduced intramembranous particles, basement membrane thickening, syncytial injury, and other signs of structural immaturity or ischemic damage, indicating that the maternal-facing trophoblast surface is profoundly altered in hypertensive disease (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:6754249, PubMed:2792915). These abnormalities are functionally important because loss or simplification of microvilli reduces exchange capacity and likely disrupts membrane-associated signaling between placenta and mother. Oxidative injury appears to be one major mechanism: microvillous plasma membranes from pregnancy-induced hypertension contain increased lipid peroxidation products and show enhanced susceptibility to oxidative stress, a state that could favor release of damaging placental factors into the maternal circulation and amplify endothelial dysfunction and vasoconstriction (PubMed:8035780). The strongest mechanistic evidence comes from the recent study showing that syncytiotrophoblasts are the predominant placental source of neprilysin, which is increased in extracellular vesicles derived from preeclamptic placentas; these vesicles enter maternal endothelial cells, degrade C-type natriuretic peptide, suppress natriuretic peptide receptor-B-mediated cyclic guanosine monophosphate production in adjacent vascular smooth muscle cells, impair uterine arterial vasodilation, and induce hypertension and proteinuria in experimental models, thereby directly connecting the syncytiotrophoblast surface compartment to the hypertensive phenotype (PubMed:40304042). In parallel, reduced syndecan-1 on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli before and during preeclampsia indicates disruption of the glycocalyx on this maternal-facing surface, and its inverse association with systolic blood pressure further supports the relevance of microvillous integrity to blood pressure regulation in pregnancy (PubMed:27299886). Broader reviews of preeclampsia also place syncytiotrophoblast stress, endothelial activation, abnormal placental signaling, and disturbed natriuretic peptide biology at the center of disease pathogenesis, which is consistent with the view that injury to the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous pathway contributes to the development and maintenance of hypertension by coupling placental malperfusion to systemic maternal vascular dysfunction (PubMed:38586611).[PubMed:40304042](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40304042) [PubMed:2627339](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2627339) [PubMed:2635867](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2635867) [PubMed:8035780](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8035780) [PubMed:38586611](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38586611) [PubMed:6754249](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6754249) [PubMed:2792915](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2792915) [PubMed:27299886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27299886) 

With this biological context in place, the enrichment result can be interpreted more coherently in relation to the published structural and mechanistic evidence.

There were 26 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[high]. This placental surface domain represents the principal maternal-facing exchange interface, and the enrichment of 26 proteins in this compartment is highly consistent with the established biology of hypertensive pregnancy, in which structural, oxidative, and signaling abnormalities converge at the syncytiotrophoblast microvillous membrane. The pathway description indicates that this membrane is essential for nutrient uptake, ion transport, peptide handling, endocrine signaling, barrier maintenance, and communication with the maternal circulation, thereby linking a single highly specialized placental surface to multiple disease-relevant processes. In hypertension, this relevance is supported by several independent lines of evidence showing reduced microvillar density, decreased intramembranous particles, diminished actin content, and broader features of syncytiotrophoblast immaturity or injury in affected placentas (PubMed:2627339, PubMed:2635867, PubMed:2792915, PubMed:6754249). Additional evidence for pathogenic involvement comes from increased lipid peroxidation in syncytiotrophoblast microvillous plasma membranes in pregnancy-induced hypertension, quantitatively reinforcing the interpretation that oxidative injury at this maternal-facing membrane contributes to placental dysfunction and maternal vascular damage (PubMed:8035780). Mechanistic extension of these observations further shows that syncytiotrophoblast-derived extracellular vesicles can transfer pathogenic cargo, including neprilysin, into the maternal circulation and directly impair vasodilatory signaling, thereby promoting hypertensive pathology (PubMed:40304042). Reduced syndecan-1 expression on syncytiotrophoblast microvilli in preeclampsia adds another layer of evidence, suggesting that disturbance of the placental glycocalyx at this surface is linked to abnormal maternal vascular adaptation (PubMed:27299886). Collectively, the enrichment of 26 proteins in this pathway provides a quantitatively focused and biologically coherent signal that hypertension-associated molecular changes are concentrated at a placental membrane domain already implicated by ultrastructural, biochemical, and mechanistic studies.

Building on this network-level view, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified in the function enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a more gene-specific manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

NOS3 stands out as the protein with the clearest and most direct relevance to hypertension because endothelial nitric oxide is a central determinant of vascular tone, arterial compliance, and blood pressure homeostasis. The provided annotation indicates that VEGF receptor signaling promotes phosphorylation of NOS3 and induces NO production in endothelial cells, while also regulating endothelial survival, permeability, and cytoskeletal organization. These processes are highly pertinent to hypertension, which is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, vascular remodeling, and altered microvascular integrity. Reduced NOS3 activity or impaired upstream activation can diminish NO bioavailability, thereby increasing vasoconstriction, promoting inflammation and platelet-endothelial interactions, and facilitating structural vascular changes that sustain elevated blood pressure. Thus, among the listed proteins, NOS3 is the strongest mechanistic link to hypertension pathogenesis through its role in endothelial signaling and NO-dependent vascular regulation.

From vascular tone regulation, it is then logical to consider proteins that may influence the contractile apparatus of the vessel wall itself.

ACTA2 is highly relevant to hypertension because smooth muscle alpha-actin is a core structural component of vascular smooth muscle cells, which determine arterial tone and vessel wall remodeling. Although the provided description is general, actin-dependent contractility and cytoskeletal dynamics are fundamentally involved in vasoconstriction, mechanotransduction, and the adaptive or maladaptive remodeling of resistance arteries in chronic hypertension. Increased vascular smooth muscle contractile activity and structural stiffening are major contributors to elevated peripheral resistance, the principal hemodynamic abnormality in essential hypertension. Therefore, ACTA2 is notable as a cytoskeletal effector that may connect cellular motility and contractile architecture to hypertensive vascular remodeling and increased arterial stiffness.

In addition to vascular contractility, endothelial handling of oxidative and lipid-related stress may also be relevant to the hypertensive state.

COLEC12 is of particular interest in hypertension because its endothelial scavenger receptor function links vascular inflammation, oxidative stress, and lipid handling. The annotation specifically notes its role in recognition, internalization, and degradation of oxidatively modified low-density lipoprotein by vascular endothelial cells. Oxidative stress and oxidized low-density lipoprotein accumulation are central features of endothelial injury and vascular inflammation, both of which contribute to reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, increased vascular stiffness, and remodeling in hypertension. Through its ability to sense modified lipids and participate in endothelial clearance pathways, COLEC12 may influence the inflammatory vascular milieu that promotes hypertensive target-organ damage and accelerates atherosclerotic complications commonly associated with high blood pressure.

A closely related consideration involves enzymes that may limit the accumulation of oxidatively damaged membrane lipids.

PLA2G15 is relevant to hypertension because phospholipid remodeling and detoxification of oxidized phospholipids are closely tied to vascular oxidative stress and inflammatory injury. The annotation highlights its ability to selectively hydrolyze truncated oxidized phospholipids and suggests a role in detoxification during oxidative stress. This is mechanistically important because oxidized phospholipids can damage endothelial cells, amplify inflammatory signaling, and impair vasodilatory responses, all of which are central to hypertensive vascular dysfunction. In addition, its broader role in membrane lipid homeostasis and intracellular lipid trafficking may influence macrophage and endothelial cell responses in cardiometabolic disease states that frequently coexist with hypertension. Hence, PLA2G15 may be a meaningful contributor to vascular injury pathways rather than a direct regulator of blood pressure itself.[PubMed:10092508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10092508) [PubMed:11790796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790796) [PubMed:20410020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20410020) [PubMed:23958596](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23958596) [PubMed:25727495](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25727495) [PubMed:29724779](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29724779) [PubMed:30830753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830753) [PubMed:36823305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) 

Beyond oxidative and lipid injury, several enriched proteins may be relevant through inflammatory and immune-mediated mechanisms.

FCN1 is noteworthy because it connects innate immune activation, complement signaling, and monocyte inflammatory responses to hypertension-related vascular disease. Chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a driver of endothelial dysfunction, arterial remodeling, and hypertensive end-organ injury. The ability of FCN1 to activate the complement lectin pathway and stimulate monocytes to secrete interleukin 8 suggests a plausible role in promoting vascular inflammation, leukocyte recruitment, and endothelial activation. While FCN1 is not a classical blood pressure regulator, its immunologic functions may be especially relevant in inflammatory or metabolic forms of hypertension, where innate immune signaling contributes to persistent vascular dysfunction.

This inflammatory theme is further extended by proteins that may restrain, rather than amplify, immune activation.

LAIR1 is potentially important in hypertension because it functions as a broad suppressor of immune-cell activation and inflammatory cytokine production. Hypertension is now widely understood to have an immune component, involving T-cell activation, cytokine-mediated vascular dysfunction, and inflammatory injury in the kidney and vasculature. The annotation indicates that LAIR1 down-regulates interleukin 2, interferon gamma, interleukin 8, interleukin 10, and tumor necrosis factor-related pathways and inhibits nuclear factor kappa B signaling, all of which are highly relevant to inflammatory amplification in hypertensive disease. Consequently, LAIR1 may represent a protective immunoregulatory axis whose reduced activity could permit excessive vascular and renal inflammation, thereby facilitating blood pressure elevation and tissue damage.

Related to this, leukocyte movement across the vascular barrier may provide another route by which immune activation contributes to hypertensive tissue injury.

CD99L2 is relevant because leukocyte transmigration across the endothelium is a key event in vascular inflammation, which contributes to endothelial dysfunction and remodeling in hypertension. The annotation specifically places CD99L2 at a late step of leukocyte extravasation, facilitating passage through the endothelial basement membrane. This function could be important in hypertensive target-organ damage, where infiltration of inflammatory cells into vascular, renal, and cardiac tissues promotes fibrosis, oxidative stress, and structural remodeling. Although CD99L2 is not a direct regulator of vascular tone, it may contribute to the inflammatory tissue environment that sustains chronic hypertension and its complications.

At a broader immunologic level, antigen presentation pathways may also shape adaptive immune responses relevant to hypertensive disease.

CD74 may have an indirect but meaningful connection to hypertension through antigen presentation and adaptive immune activation. The role of CD74 in major histocompatibility complex class two processing places it upstream of T-cell-mediated immune responses, and adaptive immunity has been implicated in the development and maintenance of hypertension, especially in relation to vascular inflammation and renal injury. Enhanced antigen presentation can promote pro-inflammatory T-cell activation, which in turn may impair endothelial function, increase oxidative stress, and contribute to sodium-retaining and vasoconstrictive states. Therefore, CD74 is relevant as part of the immunologic machinery that could shape inflammatory hypertension phenotypes.

In addition to these vascular and immune-related proteins, systemic stress-response mediators may also be informative in this enriched set.

GDF15 is of interest because it is a systemic stress signal with strong links to cardiometabolic regulation, energy balance, and disease severity. Although the annotation focuses on the GDF15-GFRAL axis in the brainstem, its induction by stressors such as cancer, drugs, and metabolic perturbation suggests broader relevance to hypertension, particularly in obesity-associated or systemic inflammatory states. Appetite suppression, altered lipid metabolism, and stress-response signaling may influence body weight, insulin sensitivity, and vascular risk, all of which modulate blood pressure. Thus, GDF15 is better viewed as a biomarker and systemic mediator of cardiometabolic stress that may accompany or modify hypertension rather than as a primary vascular effector.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) 

Finally, lipid transport and lipoprotein-associated vascular protection may provide an additional layer of contextual relevance.

APOD is potentially relevant to hypertension because high-density lipoprotein metabolism is closely related to vascular protection, oxidative balance, and endothelial health. By stabilizing high-density lipoprotein structure and influencing high-density lipoprotein metabolism, APOD may affect reverse cholesterol transport and the anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative properties of lipoproteins. These functions are important in the context of hypertension, where endothelial dysfunction and vascular stiffness are often exacerbated by dyslipidemia and oxidative stress. Although APOD is not a direct regulator of blood pressure, it may modify the vascular risk environment in which hypertension develops and contributes to cardiovascular complications.
